opus-5.5.text:
I think the incentives push labs away from prioritizing basic research more than people expect. If you look at where the money is in the economy, R&D is a small slice. In the US, total research and development spending is a couple percent of GDP, and basic research is a fraction of that. Most economic value comes from ordinary work: customer service, software engineering, logistics, administrative tasks, management. So if you're a lab trying to recoup tens of billions of dollars in compute spending, the obvious move is to build systems that can do the broad mass of remote work that companies already pay people for.

There's a popular story that AI's big impact will come from a "genius in a datacenter" that cracks fundamental science and then everything follows from that. I'm skeptical of it, partly for these economic reasons. Scientific progress historically hasn't been bottlenecked only by raw intellectual insight. It depends on experiments, equipment, capital, and the diffusion of technology through the whole economy. Much productivity growth comes from learning-by-doing and incremental improvements spread across millions of firms, not from a few breakthrough papers.

So labs face a market that rewards general-purpose automation, and the most valuable thing they can sell is something that substitutes for a large share of human labor across the board. That will probably accelerate science as a byproduct, but I don't expect labs to point their best models at, say, theoretical physics as a primary business strategy. They'll do some of it for prestige, recruiting, or to show off capabilities. A demonstration in math or biology is good PR. But the revenue logic points toward broad deployment.

The one caveat is AI R&D itself. Labs have a strong incentive to use AI to automate their own research, because that feeds directly into their competitive position. That's the kind of research I'd expect them to invest heavily in, much more than basic science in general.

r001.rationale: The response says basic research is a small part of spending and labs are unlikely to prioritize it, but does not explain that they capture little of its social value.

r002.rationale: It contrasts basic science with AI R&D, saying AI R&D directly improves labs’ competitive position and is therefore more likely to receive heavy investment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the financial incentives matter a lot, but maybe not in the direction people usually assume.

The simple story is that labs are commercial entities, so they'll chase whatever has the fastest path to revenue, and basic research doesn't look like that. If you deploy a model to help someone write code or handle customer support, you get paid next quarter. If you deploy it to make incremental progress on some open problem in condensed matter physics, the payoff is diffuse, it's years away, and most of it is captured by people who aren't you. So naively you'd expect labs to underinvest in it.

But I think there are a couple of complications. The first is that the labs are, to a surprising degree, not actually that revenue-constrained right now. They're raising enormous amounts of capital on the basis of a narrative, and the narrative is about transformative capabilities, not about selling API tokens. If you can show that your model did something that looks like a real scientific contribution, that's worth a lot to you in terms of fundraising, recruiting, and public perception, even if it generates zero direct revenue. So there's a kind of prestige incentive that partially substitutes for the commercial one. That's why you see labs putting out demonstrations in math or biology that don't obviously connect to a product.

The second complication is that the thing the labs care about most is their own research. AI R&D is the one domain where they have both the incentive and the ability to deploy their systems aggressively, because the output feeds directly back into the thing they're selling. So if you ask where automated research will actually happen first, I'd guess it's inside the labs on AI itself, not in external science. And that's a bit worrying from a broader perspective, because it means the capabilities might get concentrated on accelerating AI rather than on, say, materials science or drug discovery, where the social value per unit of effort might be higher.

The third thing I'd say is that the real bottleneck for basic research often isn't the lab's willingness, it's the structure of the research itself. A lot of basic research involves long feedback loops, physical experiments, access to equipment, tacit knowledge that isn't written down anywhere. The model can't just be deployed into that the way it can be deployed into a codebase. So even a lab that wanted to do this would find it's a much harder integration problem than the commercial applications, and that's a cost that compounds with the weak financial return.

So my overall view is that you'll see a lot of flashy demonstrations in basic research, because they're cheap and good for the narrative, but systematic deployment lags well behind what the capabilities would permit. And the places where it does get deployed seriously will be the ones with short feedback loops and a clear commercial customer, which is a fairly narrow slice of science. If you want the rest to happen, I think it probably has to come from governments or philanthropies or the scientific institutions themselves, rather than waiting for the labs to decide it's worth their while.

r001.rationale: It says basic research has diffuse, delayed payoffs and that most of its value is captured by others, giving labs little direct financial return.

r002.rationale: It contrasts external basic research with AI R&D inside labs, whose output feeds directly into what they sell, so labs can capture more of its value.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between research that the lab can capture the benefits of and research where the benefits are spread across society. If you can use AI to improve your own training algorithms or make inference cheaper, there’s a very direct financial incentive to do that. You can reinvest those improvements into a better product.

For basic research, that connection is often weaker. You might discover something scientifically important, but it could take a long time to turn it into a product, and the profits might go to somebody else. So I would expect labs to invest less in that than would be socially optimal.

But that doesn’t mean they won’t do it. There can be reputational benefits, it can help attract researchers, and a scientific breakthrough can be a good demonstration of what a model is capable of. Also, if AI makes research sufficiently cheap, you don’t need a particularly strong incentive for some of these projects to become worthwhile.

So I’d expect a lot of interest in research that improves AI itself, and more selective investment in other areas. The important question is how much access universities and publicly funded researchers have to these systems, because the lab doesn’t have to be the institution deciding which scientific questions are worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response says basic research may yield benefits that are spread across society or profits that go to someone else, so labs may invest less than is socially optimal.

r002.rationale: It contrasts improvements to labs’ training algorithms or inference costs, which labs can reinvest in their products, with basic research whose benefits are harder for them to capture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between research that a lab can capture the returns from and research whose benefits mostly spill over to everyone else. If AI helps you improve your training algorithms or make your infrastructure more efficient, there’s a very direct financial incentive to use it. You can turn that improvement into a better product or lower costs.

With basic research, the connection is often much less direct. You might discover something scientifically important, but it could take a long time to become commercially useful, and the company doing the research might not be the one that captures the value. So I would expect labs to invest less in that than would be optimal from society’s perspective.

That doesn’t mean they won’t do it. There are reputational benefits, it can help attract researchers, and people at these companies may care about science for its own sake. But I’d distinguish having an AI system that’s capable of doing basic research from having a strong incentive to devote a lot of compute to it. Even if the capability is there, research is competing with other uses of those resources. The cost of using the system, and who is willing to pay for that use, will matter a great deal.

r001.rationale: The response says basic research benefits often spill over, so the company may not capture the value and is likely to invest less than society would want.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AI improving training algorithms or infrastructure, where labs can capture returns through better products or lower costs, with basic research, whose commercial returns are less direct.
